hazards.heavier-cannot-fly: You said the aircraft is too heavy to fly. It is heavy, but its wings push a huge amount of air downward every second as it moves, and the air pushes the wings up just as hard. Enough speed and the right wing shape make lift greater than weight.
hazards.leave-a-pen-on-the-apron: You left a pen on the apron. Loose objects on the ground can be sucked into an engine or thrown by the wind from a propeller. Crews walk the apron looking for anything loose, so keep everything you carry in your pocket.
hazards.push-a-control-surface: You reached to push a flap. Control surfaces are set and checked by the mechanics, and a pushed flap can hide damage or catch a hand. Look with your eyes, and let the mechanic move and inspect them.
hazards.walk-under-a-propeller: You headed for the front of the propeller. A propeller can be hard to see when it spins, and even a still one should never be touched or walked in front of. On the apron, people walk only where the ground crew shows them, well away from propellers and engine intakes.

interrupts.alert: A tug starts to back an aircraft out through the hangar door.
interrupts.cue: Stand still on the painted walkway and wait until the tug and aircraft are clear.
interrupts.missNote: The class kept walking toward the door as the aircraft came out.
interrupts.why: A tug driver pushing an aircraft backward cannot see everything behind the wings. Staying still on the walkway keeps you where the wing walker and driver expect people to be. Ground crews stop and wait for moving aircraft every day.
interrupts.wrongNote: That puts the class in the aircraft's path. Stand still on the walkway. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: The mechanic asks why the flaps come down before landing.
interrupts.cue: Say the flaps change the wing's shape to give more lift at slow speed.
interrupts.missNote: You could not say what the flaps do, and the mechanic explained before the class went on.
interrupts.why: Landing means flying slowly, and slow air gives less lift. Flaps make up for it. Knowing that shows why a stuck flap is something the mechanic will always fix before flight.
interrupts.wrongNote: That does not explain the flaps. Say what they do at slow speed. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.lkf-checkin: The check-in comes at the end, by the hangar door.
lateNotes.lkf-lift-log: The lift table is written once you have tested the angles — nothing to record yet.

name: How a Wing Lifts an Aircraft

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Mark lift, weight and thrust on the model aircraft.

decoyNotes.lkf-sock: It shows the wind on the field, not a force on the aircraft.

itemNames.lkf-lift: lift, pushing up on the wings

itemNotes.lkf-lift: Comes from air moving over the wings.
itemNotes.lkf-weight: Gravity on the aircraft and its load.

steps.prompt: Mark lift, weight and thrust on the model aircraft.
steps.title: Find the four forces on the aircraft
steps.why: Four forces act on every aircraft in flight. Lift pushes up and comes from the wings. Weight pulls down toward the ground. Thrust pushes forward and comes from the engines or propellers. Drag holds the aircraft back as it pushes through the air. The aircraft climbs, cruises or lands depending on which forces are stronger.

steps.cue: Follow the aircraft mechanic along the painted walkway into the hangar.
steps.prompt: Follow the aircraft mechanic along the painted walkway into the hangar.
steps.title: Walk the painted path with the mechanic
steps.why: An airport apron is busy, with aircraft, tugs and fuel trucks moving about. Painted walkways show where people on foot are expected, so drivers and pilots know where to look for them. Staying on the path with the mechanic keeps the class where the ground crew can see everyone at all times.

steps.cue: Order what happens as the aircraft goes from standing still to climbing.

itemNames.lkf-ord-climb: 4 · the wheels lift and it climbs
itemNames.lkf-ord-thrust: 1 · engines give thrust and it rolls

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. The engines give thrust first, before there is any speed or lift.
steps.prompt: Order what happens as the aircraft goes from standing still to climbing.
steps.title: Put the takeoff forces in order
steps.why: Takeoff is a story about forces changing. The engines give thrust and the aircraft rolls faster down the runway. As its speed grows, air moves faster over the wings and lift grows. When lift becomes greater than weight, the wheels leave the ground. Then the pilot keeps enough thrust to beat drag and keep climbing.

steps.cue: Hold the model wing steady in the airflow until the lift scale settles.
steps.holdBreakNote: The wing wobbled and the reading jumped. Hold it steady again and wait.
steps.prompt: Hold the model wing steady in the airflow until the lift scale settles.
steps.title: Hold the wing steady in the wind tunnel
steps.why: A wind tunnel blows air past a model so scientists can measure the forces on it. Holding the wing steady lets the lift reading settle to one value. If the wing wobbles, the reading jumps about and cannot be trusted. Engineers test wing shapes this way long before a real aircraft is built.

steps.cue: Turn the angle knob to tilt the wing's front edge up until the lift scale rises.
steps.prompt: Turn the angle knob to tilt the wing's front edge up until the lift scale rises.
steps.title: Tilt the wing to find more lift
steps.why: Tilting the front of the wing up a little makes it push more air downward, so the air pushes the wing up harder. That tilt is called the angle of attack. Tilt it too far and the smooth airflow breaks away from the top of the wing and lift drops suddenly. Pilots and designers keep the angle in the safe range.

steps.cue: Commit when the marker sits at the reading on the wind tunnel's lift scale.

gauge.label: LIFT
gauge.missNote: Not at the reading yet. Read where the needle points on the scale.

steps.prompt: Commit when the marker sits at the reading on the wind tunnel's lift scale.
steps.title: Read the lift on the scale
steps.why: The scale measures how hard the air pushes the model wing up. Reading it at each angle lets you compare one setting with another. That comparison is how you find the angle that gives the most lift before the airflow breaks away. Measuring, not guessing, is how engineers learn what a wing can do.

steps.cue: Drag the model flap down to its landing position at the back of the wing.

drag.missNote: Not at the landing position yet. Set the flap fully down.

steps.prompt: Drag the model flap down to its landing position at the back of the wing.
steps.title: Set the flap down for landing
steps.why: Flaps slide out and down from the back of the wing. They change the wing's shape so it makes more lift at slow speed, which lets the aircraft land gently on a runway of normal length. They also add drag to help slow it down. That is why mechanics check that every flap moves freely before each flight.

steps.cue: Choose the sentence that explains how something so heavy gets off the ground.
steps.prompt: Choose the sentence that explains how something so heavy gets off the ground.
steps.title: Say why the aircraft can fly
steps.why: You saw lift grow with speed and with the wing's tilt. A good answer says that the moving wing pushes air downward and the air pushes the wing up, and when that lift is bigger than the weight, the aircraft rises. It uses the forces you measured and nothing more.

steps.cue: Walk round the parked aircraft with the mechanic and mark the three things checked.

decoyNotes.lkf-logo: Nice paint, but not a safety check.

itemNames.lkf-cover: the red cover on a sensor

steps.prompt: Walk round the parked aircraft with the mechanic and mark the three things checked.
steps.title: Spot what the mechanic checks on the walk-round
steps.why: Before every flight a mechanic walks all the way round the aircraft. Tyres must be in good shape for landing. Control surfaces must move freely and be undamaged. Covers on sensors and intakes must be taken off. A careful walk-round catches small problems on the ground, where they are easy and safe to fix.

steps.cue: Keep the marker on the smoke trail as it flows over the top of the wing.
steps.holdBreakNote: The marker lost the smoke. Find the trail again and follow it over the wing.
steps.prompt: Keep the marker on the smoke trail as it flows over the top of the wing.
steps.title: Follow the smoke over the wing
steps.why: A thin line of smoke in the wind tunnel shows exactly how the air moves. Over a working wing it curves smoothly along the top and leaves the back edge heading downward. That downward push of air is the partner of lift. If you tilt the wing too far, the smoke tears away into swirls, and you can see lift being lost.

steps.cue: Write a line for a small tilt, a medium tilt and a steep tilt.
steps.prompt: Write a line for a small tilt, a medium tilt and a steep tilt.
steps.title: Record lift at each angle
steps.why: A record of lift at three angles shows the pattern in one glance: more tilt gives more lift, until too much tilt makes it fall away. A simple table like this is what test engineers build from wind tunnel runs, and pilots learn the same pattern so they never tilt too far.

steps.cue: Hand your lift table to the mechanic and point to the angle where lift fell away.
steps.prompt: Hand your lift table to the mechanic and point to the angle where lift fell away.
steps.title: Show your table to the mechanic
steps.why: Showing your results to someone who works with aircraft every day is a real test. The mechanic can tell you whether your pattern matches what happens on a real wing. Mechanics sign their work so the next person can trust it, and your table is your own signed record.

steps.cue: Name the four forces. What happens if the wing is tilted too far?
steps.prompt: Name the four forces. What happens if the wing is tilted too far?
steps.title: Check in at the hangar door
steps.why: The mechanic ends the visit by asking what stuck. Each learner names the forces and says what a too-steep tilt does to the airflow. If anyone still thinks a heavy aircraft simply cannot fly, the class talks it through at the door.
